questions.q: You run 50 independent hypothesis tests, each at α = 0.05, and every null hypothesis is actually true. Approximately what is the family-wise error rate (probability of at least one false positive)?
questions.explain: FWER = 1 − (1 − 0.05)^50 ≈ 1 − 0.95^50 ≈ 1 − 0.0769 ≈ 0.923, or about 92% — almost certain to see at least one false positive by chance alone.

questions.q: How does the Bonferroni correction decide whether to reject hypothesis i, when testing m hypotheses at overall level α?
options: Reject only the single hypothesis with the smallest p-value
questions.explain: Bonferroni uses a stricter per-test threshold of α/m. By the union bound, this guarantees the family-wise error rate stays at or below α, regardless of dependence between tests.

questions.q: What does the false discovery rate (FDR) measure, as controlled by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure?
options: The probability that at least one test among all m is a false positive
The expected proportion of false positives among the hypotheses that were actually rejected
The total number of hypotheses tested
The probability that every rejected hypothesis is a true positive
questions.explain: FDR is the expected proportion of false positives among the rejected (declared significant) hypotheses specifically — not among all hypotheses tested, and not the probability of any single false positive occurring.

questions.q: Compared to Bonferroni, why is the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure often preferred when screening many candidate trading strategies?
options: It controls a stricter error rate than Bonferroni
It is generally less conservative, giving more statistical power to detect real effects while still controlling the expected false-discovery proportion
It requires no significance level to be chosen at all
It eliminates the need for p-values entirely
questions.explain: Benjamini-Hochberg controls a less strict quantity (FDR instead of FWER), which makes it less conservative than Bonferroni and gives it more power to flag genuinely significant results amid many tests — important when you expect some real effects among many candidates.

questions.q: A researcher backtests 2,000 trading strategies, all built from random noise with zero true edge, at an uncorrected α = 0.05 per test. Roughly how many would be expected to appear 'significant' by chance alone?
questions.explain: With every null hypothesis true, the expected number of false positives at the 5% level is simply m × α = 2000 × 0.05 = 100 — a direct illustration of why uncorrected multiple testing on many backtested strategies is dangerous.
